paras: The killing of Ben Scott was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Constable Meek and Deputy Hanes during an attempted arrest at his home eight miles north of Mount Pleasant, Texas, on the night of 19 August 1905. Scott surrendered after he was wounded and died in the county jail the next night. The only report found, a Mount Pleasant dispatch, gave the officers' account that he had fired first.

The officers had gone to arrest Scott on a charge of assault to murder against his wife. According to the dispatch, he had lived in the county for two years but had never been to town, and in that way had avoided the officers.

Scott was not at home when the officers reached his house, but he arrived while they were there. In the officers' version, he ran inside, got a pistol and "opened fire" from the door, and in the "regular battle" that followed he emptied his pistol while the officers "fired a number of shots each." Once wounded and out of ammunition, he ran to a nearby house to get a Winchester, failed, and surrendered. He was jailed in town and died there on Sunday night.

Before he died, it was reported, he was found to have gone by another name, probably John Johnson or Sam Brown, and was believed wanted in Louisiana for the murder of a white man. A Black woman who lived with him said his real name was Sam Brown and that he was wanted near Shreveport for killing a white man. No report of an inquest appears in the coverage.

The Waxahachie Daily Light ran the dispatch on its front page on 22 August under the headline "IS KILLED BY DEPUTIES" and the deck "Negro Resisted Officers at Mt. Pleasant and Received Fatal Wounds." The story gave the officers' version as fact and added his old bullet wounds, his aliases and the suspicion that he had killed a white man. No other white paper's report was found, and no Black newspaper in the coverage mentioned the shooting.

reader.title: Killing of Ben Scott
bases: Two officers shot Scott while trying to arrest him on an assault charge, and he died of the wound in jail; no crowd or mob is mentioned (A1).
One white-press dispatch is the only report found; it gives the officers' version, and nothing in the Black press was found (A1).
